category_name: Unpaid carers and the care workforce

posts.title: Strain, not caring itself
posts.insight: In the study usually cited for caring shortening life, higher mortality appeared only in spouse carers who reported strain; later population studies found carers as a whole lived as long as or longer than non-carers.
posts.angle: Correct a common reading of Schulz and Beach 1999: the risk marker is reported strain, not the carer role. Position: ask every carer about strain and target support there.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Schulz and Beach 1999; Roth et al. 2015 review) and clinical interpretation (ask about strain and prioritise support accordingly)

captions.x:
A 1999 study is widely cited as evidence that caring for a spouse is bad for your health. Read the detail.

In 392 US spouse carers and 427 non-carers aged 66 to 96, the higher death rate over 4 years was seen only in carers who said caring caused them mental or emotional strain. The estimate was borderline. Carers without strain did not show a clear difference from non-carers.

A later review found five population studies in which carers as a whole lived as long as or longer than non-carers. That does not show caring protects health: healthier people may be the ones who take it on.

Ask every carer directly about strain. Offer support first to those who report it.
captions.linkedin:
A 1999 study is widely cited as evidence that caring for a spouse is bad for your health. The detail supports a narrower reading.

Schulz and Beach followed 392 spouse carers and 427 non-carers aged 66 to 96 in four US communities for about 4 years. The higher adjusted death rate was seen only in carers who reported mental or emotional strain from caring (relative risk 1.63; the lower end of the confidence interval was 1.00, so the finding is borderline).

Carers who reported no strain did not show a clear difference from non-carers.

A 2015 review by Roth, Fredman and Haley then found five later population studies in which carers as a whole had lower mortality, living as long as or longer than non-carers. Most carers in those studies also reported some benefit from caring, and many reported little or no strain.

None of this shows that caring protects health. These are observational studies, and healthier people may be the ones who take on caring.

The clinical reading I take from it: being a carer is not by itself a marker of risk. Reported strain is the more useful signal.

So ask every carer directly whether caring is causing them strain, record the answer, and offer support first to those who say yes.
captions.bluesky:
The 1999 study often cited as showing that caring for a spouse harms health found higher 4-year mortality only in carers reporting strain, and that result was borderline. Later population studies found carers overall lived as long or longer.

Ask carers about strain; support those who report it.

posts.title: Two questions to judge a break
posts.insight: Trials of respite for dementia carers are few and very low quality, so the lack of shown benefit is a research gap. Carers' own accounts suggest a break works when the carer believes the person is benefiting too.
posts.angle: Replace 'does respite work?' with two questions a family can answer: did the carer rest, and did the person find it acceptable?
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Cochrane review; concept analysis) and ethical judgement (thin trial evidence is no reason to withhold breaks)

captions.x:
How do you tell whether a break from caring has worked?

A Cochrane review of respite for carers of people with dementia found only 4 trials (753 people), with very low quality evidence. They did not show a clear benefit. That is a gap in the research, not proof that breaks do not help.

Studies of carers' own experiences suggest a break feels like real rest when the carer believes the person they look after is getting something from it too.

So judge a break by two questions. Did you actually rest? Did the person enjoy it, or at least find it tolerable?

Thin trial evidence is no reason to withhold breaks.
captions.linkedin:
How do you tell whether a break from caring has worked?

The trial evidence gives little help. A Cochrane review of respite care for people with dementia and their carers found only 4 trials, with 753 participants. The quality of evidence was very low. The trials did not show a clear benefit for carers.

The review authors cautioned that this may reflect the lack of good research rather than a real lack of benefit. An absence of evidence is different from evidence that breaks do not help. The review dates from 2014 and no update was found.

A second kind of research asks carers what a break means to them. A concept analysis of that literature described respite as two things: a service that gives a physical break, and a mental break for the carer. A positive experience depended on the carer believing that the person they care for was benefiting too.

That suggests two practical questions for carers, and for the services that arrange breaks:

1. Did the carer actually rest?
2. Did the person being cared for enjoy it, or at least find it tolerable?

If the answer to the second is no, many carers will not rest either.

My judgement: we should not withhold breaks because the trials are few. We should arrange them in a way that answers both questions, and ask both after every break.
captions.bluesky:
Only 4 trials have tested respite breaks for carers of people with dementia, and the evidence is very low quality. No clear benefit shown, but that is a research gap.

Carers say a break feels restful when the person benefits too.

Ask: did I rest? Did they find it OK?
captions.threads:

posts.title: What should carer support be judged by?
posts.insight: A UK coping programme improved carers' anxiety and depression for six years but showed no clear difference in care home timing; a US counselling programme was linked with a later nursing home move. Which outcome counts is a choice.
posts.angle: Carer support should be judged first by the carer's health and quality of life; care home timing is not automatically a success or failure.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical findings (START 6-year follow-up; Mittelman 2006) and ethical judgement (which outcome to value)

captions.x:
Two trials of support for family carers of people with dementia can be judged by different yardsticks.

In a UK trial of 260 carers, an eight-session coping programme called START left carers with fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression than usual care, lasting six years. The average difference was modest. It did not show a clear difference in how soon the person moved into a care home, though the uncertainty was wide.

In a separate US trial of 406 spouse carers, counselling and support was linked with a later nursing home move, by an estimated 557 days.

My view: judge carer support first by the carer's health. A later care home move is not automatically the better outcome.
captions.linkedin:
Two trials of support for family carers of people with dementia can be judged by different yardsticks.

START, a UK trial, randomised 260 family carers to an eight-session coping programme delivered by supervised psychology graduates, or to usual care. Over six years, carers who had START had fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression. The average difference was modest: about 2 points on a 42-point scale.

START did not show a clear difference in how soon the person with dementia moved into a care home. The uncertainty around that result was wide, so it is not evidence of no effect.

A separate US trial of 406 spouse carers of people with Alzheimer's disease tested counselling and support. It was linked with a later move to a nursing home: a statistical model estimated the typical delay at 557 days, about 18 months.

These trials differ in country, era, population and programme, so they should not be compared head to head.

They do show a choice. A programme can be counted a success because the carer is less anxious and depressed, or because the person stays at home longer.

My judgement: carer support should be judged first by the carer's own health and quality of life. A later care home move is not automatically the better outcome, and an earlier one is not automatically a failure. Sometimes a move is the right decision for both people.

When you read an evaluation of carer support, check which outcome it treats as the main one.
captions.bluesky:

posts.title: Relief after the death
posts.insight: In a US study of 217 dementia carers, 72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them, and on average depressive symptoms fell within three months; support was needed most before the death.
posts.angle: Speak about relief openly, and put carer support into the caring years rather than only after the death.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Schulz et al. NEJM 2003) and ethical judgement (relief should be spoken about; timing of support)

captions.x:
Feeling relief when someone you cared for with dementia dies is common.

In a US study of 217 family carers of people with dementia, 72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them. More than 90 in 100 believed it was a relief to the person who died.

On average, carers' symptoms of depression fell within three months of the death. The researchers concluded that carers needed support most before the death, during the caring years.

This was one US study, and averages hide people who grieve differently.

If you felt relief, you can say so to your GP or to anyone supporting you. And if you are caring now, ask for support now.
captions.linkedin:
Feeling relief when someone you cared for with dementia dies is common.

A US study followed 217 family carers of people with dementia who died. The carers were part of a larger research programme. Half of them had spent at least 46 hours a week caring in the year before the death.

72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them. More than 90 in 100 believed it was a relief to the person who died.

On average, carers' symptoms of depression fell within three months of the death. Within a year they were substantially lower than during the caring years.

The researchers concluded that carers needed support most before the death.

Some limits: this was one US sample, the feelings were self-reported, and averages hide people whose grief follows a different pattern.

Two things follow, in my judgement.

Relief is a common response after long and demanding care, and it should be possible to say so without being judged. Relief and grief can be felt together.

Support for carers should be concentrated during the caring years, when the study found it was needed most, and not saved for after the death.

If you are caring for someone now, ask your GP or local carers' service what support is available to you now.
captions.bluesky:
In a US study of 217 family carers of people with dementia, 72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them. On average their depressive symptoms fell within three months.

Relief is common and can be said aloud. If you are caring now, ask for support now.

posts.title: Hand over to the carer at discharge
posts.insight: Randomised trials of discharge planning that brought family carers in found about a quarter fewer readmissions over 3 to 6 months (relative). The programmes used written plans, links to services, demonstration and teach-back.
posts.angle: Treat the family carer as a recipient of the discharge handover, built from the components the trials used.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Rodakowski meta-analysis) and clinical interpretation (a carer handover checklist built from trial components)

captions.x:
Hand over to the family carer at discharge with the same care you give the GP letter.

A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials of older adults going home found that discharge planning which brought carers in was linked with about a quarter fewer readmissions over 3 to 6 months. That is a relative reduction, pooled from 6 and 5 trials.

The programmes had several parts, so no single part can be credited. Common ones: a written care plan, links to community services, showing the carer how to do care tasks, and asking them to show it back.

Start with those four before the person leaves.
captions.linkedin:
Hand over to the family carer at discharge with the same care you give the GP letter.

Rodakowski and colleagues pooled 15 randomised trials, including 4361 older adults discharged from hospital or skilled nursing care to the community with an informal carer.

Discharge planning that brought carers in was linked with about a quarter fewer readmissions at 90 days (6 trials) and 180 days (5 trials). These are relative reductions; absolute rates were not available, so I will not turn them into a number in 100. Many trials were unclear about allocation concealment and blinding.

The programmes had several parts, and the authors could not say which part worked. The components the trials used most often were:

1. Linking carers to community services (13 of 15 trials).
2. A written care plan (9 of 15).
3. Assessing the carer (8 of 15).
4. Asking the carer to show back what they had been taught (7 of 15).
5. Live or video demonstration of care tasks (5 of 15).

My clinical reading: the family carer is often the person who will give most of the care in the first weeks at home. They should receive a handover addressed to them, not a copy of someone else's.

A practical version before the person leaves: a written summary for the carer, contact details for the services you have linked them to, and a supervised practice of any new task, with the carer doing it while a nurse or therapist watches.
captions.bluesky:
Trials of discharge planning that brought family carers in found about a quarter fewer readmissions over 3 to 6 months (relative).

Common parts: a written plan, links to services, demonstrating tasks, and the carer showing them back.

Give the carer a handover of their own.
captions.threads:

A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials found discharge planning that brought carers in was linked with about a quarter fewer readmissions over 3 to 6 months. That is relative, and the programmes had several parts.

posts.title: When a home care client dies
posts.insight: Home care workers described losing a relationship and, in New York, paid work when a client died; in England, peer support, manager acknowledgement, time off and encouragement to attend the funeral helped.
posts.angle: Agencies should treat a client's death as a loss for the worker: tell them personally and promptly, acknowledge it, and allow time for the funeral where the family welcome it.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical findings (two qualitative studies) and ethical judgement (what agencies should do)

captions.x:
In a New York study, home care workers described losing two things when a client died: a close relationship, and paid work. They felt employers and society underestimated that loss.

In interviews with 29 home care workers and 13 managers in England, workers said a client's death could leave them drained and under-prepared. What helped: support from experienced colleagues, managers acknowledging their feelings, and for some, time off or encouragement to attend the funeral.

Both studies were small and qualitative.

My judgement: agencies should tell a worker about a client's death personally and promptly, and allow time for the funeral where the family welcome it.
captions.linkedin:
In a New York study, home care workers described losing two things when a client died: a close relationship, and paid work. The researchers concluded that workers' grief went unrecognised, because employers and society underestimated both the relationship and the loss.

That job-loss finding comes from the US. I have no verified data on how often it happens in England, so I will not claim it does.

An English study interviewed 29 home care workers and 13 home care managers about caring for people with dementia at the end of life. Workers said that a client's death, or being caught up in family conflict, could leave them emotionally drained, under-prepared and overwhelmed.

They described what helped:

1. Encouragement and learning from experienced colleagues.
2. Managers at their agency acknowledging their feelings.
3. For some, time off or encouragement to attend the client's funeral.

Both studies are qualitative. They describe what workers experienced and valued; they do not test any intervention.

My judgement, which goes beyond the studies: an agency should tell a worker about a client's death personally and promptly, not through a changed rota. It should acknowledge the loss. Where the family welcome it, it should allow time to attend the funeral.

We should treat the end of that relationship as a loss.
captions.bluesky:
Home care workers in England said a client's death could leave them drained and under-prepared. What helped: experienced colleagues, managers acknowledging their feelings, time off or going to the funeral.

Agencies should tell workers personally and promptly.
captions.threads:
In a New York study, home care workers described losing a close relationship and paid work when a client died.

In England, 29 workers and 13 managers described feeling drained and under-prepared after a death. Support from colleagues, managers acknowledging feelings, and time off or going to the funeral helped.

Small qualitative studies. My view: agencies should tell workers about a death personally and promptly.

items: Panel 1: The manager phones the worker before her next shift. "I wanted you to hear it from me. Mrs Okafor died this morning."
Panel 2: Two colleagues sit with her on a break. "The first one is hard. Tell me about her."
Panel 3: The worker, in dark clothes, stands at the back of a funeral gathering; the family have invited her.
text.source_line: Yeh et al., Int J Geriatr Psychiatry 2019; Tsui et al., Qual Health Res 2019

Panel 2: a small staff room, two older colleagues (one white man in his sixties, one Black woman in her fifties) seated with her, mugs on the table. Panel 3: outdoor funeral gathering, family at front, the worker at the back with a colleague. Captions sit under panels; no text inside the drawings.

posts.title: Listening is not disclosing
posts.insight: Carers are often refused information on grounds of consent; listening to a carer shares nothing, and asking the patient who may be told resolves much of the rest.
posts.angle: Separate two acts: always listen to carers; separately ask the patient what may be shared and with whom, and record it.
posts.position_basis: mixed: empirical finding (Irish carer survey) and clinical interpretation (listen always; ask and record sharing preferences)

captions.x:
Over half of carers in an Irish survey had struggled to get information from the care team. The commonest reason they were given was that the patient had not consented.

That was 159 carers of people with mental illness, recruited through a support group, so it is not a sample of older people's services.

Two separate acts get merged here. Listening to what a carer tells you shares nothing about the patient. Always listen.

Then, while the patient can answer, ask what may be shared and with whom. Record the answer where the next clinician will find it.
captions.linkedin:
Over half of carers in an Irish survey had struggled to get information from the treating team. The commonest reason they were given was lack of the patient's consent.

The survey included 159 carers of people with mental illness, recruited through a support group. It was self-selected, from one country and from mental health services, not older people's services. I use it as a signal, not as a measure of practice in geriatric medicine.

The teaching point is a distinction that gets lost on busy wards.

Listening to a carer and telling a carer are two different acts. Listening shares nothing about the patient. What the carer tells you about how the person was last week, what they eat, how they sleep, and what has changed is often the best history available.

So:

1. Always listen to carers, whatever has been agreed about sharing.
2. Separately, ask the patient, while they are able to answer, what may be shared and with whom.
3. Record that answer in a place the next clinician will look, so the carer is not refused again on the next shift.

If the patient is unable to decide, the usual approach to acting in their best interests applies, and that includes hearing from the people who know them.

Listening breaches no confidence, and it often gives you the history you need.
captions.bluesky:
Over half of 159 carers in an Irish mental health survey struggled to get information from care teams, most often told the patient had not consented.

Listening to a carer shares nothing. Always listen. Separately, ask the patient who may be told, and record it.

posts.title: A one-page plan if you, the carer, are suddenly ill
posts.insight: If you care for someone, a one-page plan written in advance and shared with named people lets someone else step in quickly if you are suddenly unwell.
posts.angle: Practical advice: write the plan now, share it, and ask about emergency planning at a carer's assessment.
posts.position_basis: practical advice (clinical interpretation); no empirical claim

captions.x:
If you care for someone, write down on one page what they would need if you were suddenly taken ill.

Keep it simple: their medicines and when they take them, what they need help with, their daily routine, who to call, and where the spare keys are.

Give a copy to one or two people who could step in, and keep one by the front door or in your bag.

If you have a carer's assessment (a meeting with the council about your own needs as a carer), ask them to go through the plan with you.

Then someone else can step in quickly, knowing what the person needs.
captions.linkedin:
If you care for someone, write down on one page what they would need if you were suddenly taken ill.

You may be the only person who knows which tablets go in the morning, how the person likes their tea, or what calms them if they are upset. If you are taken into hospital without warning, someone else has to find all of that out.

A one-page plan written in advance means they do not have to guess. It could include:

1. The person's medicines, doses and times, and where they are kept.
2. What they need help with: washing, dressing, meals, getting to the toilet, moving about.
3. Their usual daily routine and anything that upsets or settles them.
4. Who to call: family, friends, GP, any home care agency.
5. Where the spare keys are, and how to get into the house.

Give a copy to one or two named people who could step in, and tell them where the original is kept. Keep a note in your wallet or bag saying that you are a carer and who to contact.

If you have a carer's assessment (a meeting with your council about your own needs as a carer), ask them to go through the plan with you and say what help could be arranged in an emergency.

Review it when anything changes, such as a new medicine.

More posts in the Ask this series take one practical question at a time.
